title: What is the ‘Base Amount’ in R&D tax credit calculations?
description: The R&D tax credit base amount is the threshold that a taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) must exceed under IRC § 41.
summary: The R&D tax credit base amount is the threshold that a taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) must exceed under IRC § 41. Under the Regular Research Credit for U.S. taxpayers, it equals the fixed-base percentage, capped at 16%, times average gross receipts for the prior four years, but never less than 50% of current-year QREs.

body.text: The R&D tax credit base amount is the threshold that a taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) must exceed under IRC § 41. Under the Regular Research Credit for U.S. taxpayers, it equals the fixed-base percentage, capped at 16%, times average gross receipts for the prior four years, but never less than 50% of current-year QREs.
Law and guidance reflect authoritative primary federal and state tax sources current through November 11, 2026. This report is informational and is not legal or tax advice.
1. The base amount in one paragraph

Under the Regular Research Credit (RRC), the credit is 20 percent of the amount by which a taxpayer’s current-year qualified research expenses (QREs) exceed a "base amount" (IRC § 41(a)(1)). The base amount is the taxpayer’s Fixed-Base Percentage (FBP) multiplied by its average annual gross receipts for the four taxable years preceding the credit year (IRC § 41(c)(1)). Two limits apply: the FBP may not exceed 16 percent (IRC § 41(c)(3)(C)), and the base amount may never be less than 50 percent of current-year QREs (IRC § 41(c)(2)). Only QREs above the base amount earn the credit, which is how the statute rewards increases in research spending rather than all research spending. In addition, if the credit year is a short taxable year, the base amount determined under IRC § 41(c)(1) is modified by multiplying that amount by the number of months in the short taxable year and dividing the result by 12, though it still cannot be reduced below 50 percent of current-year QREs (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(b)(1)).
2. The formula, step by step

cells: Fixed-Base Percentage = aggregate QREs ÷ aggregate gross receipts for the base period (1984–1988 for established taxpayers; start-up rules otherwise), capped at 16% and rounded to the nearest 1/100th of 1%
Average annual gross receipts for the 4 taxable years preceding the credit year
Base amount = the greater of Step 3 or 50% of current-year QREs
Excess QREs = current-year QREs − base amount

body.text: 2.1 What goes into QREs (the numerator and the current-year figure)

QREs are the sum of in-house research expenses and contract research expenses (IRC § 41(b)(1)). In-house expenses are wages for qualified services, supplies used in qualified research, and certain amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)). Contract research expenses are generally counted at 65 percent of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for qualified research, or 75 percent and 100 percent for amounts paid to certain qualified research consortia, eligible small businesses, universities, and federal laboratories (IRC § 41(b)(3)).

To be QREs, the costs must relate to "qualified research" under IRC § 41(d)(1): the expenditures must be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)); the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information which is technological in nature, and the application of which is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (a product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention) (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B), (d)(2)(B)); and substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified functional purpose relating to a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), (d)(3)(A)).
Pub. L. 119–21 (enacted July 4, 2025) amended IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) so that it now refers to domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A.
3. The Fixed-Base Percentage
3.1 Established taxpayers: the 1984–1988 base period

For taxpayers that are not start-up companies, the FBP is the percentage which the aggregate QREs of the taxpayer for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989, is of the aggregate gross receipts of the taxpayer for such taxable years (IRC § 41(c)(3)(A); IRS Audit Techniques Guide, research credit computation). Once determined, that ratio is applied in every later credit year, subject only to adjustments required by the consistency rule under IRC § 41(c)(5) or acquisition and disposition rules under IRC § 41(f)(3).
3.2 Start-up companies

A taxpayer is treated as a start-up company if the first taxable year in which it had both gross receipts and QREs began after December 31, 1983, or if there were fewer than three taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989, in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and QREs (IRC § 41(c)(3)(B)(i)). Its FBP follows a statutory phase-in schedule, counted from the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 1993, for which the taxpayer has QREs (IRC § 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)):

headers: Credit year (counted from first post-1993 year with QREs)
Years whose QRE-to-gross-receipts ratio is used

cells: Any 5 years the taxpayer selects from years 5 through 10

body.text: The IRS Audit Techniques Guide adds that a company spun off or formed from an existing business may be required under the IRC § 41(f)(3) successor rules to carry over its predecessor’s base-period history and therefore may not qualify as a start-up company. Furthermore, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(b)(3), no adjustment is made to the computation of a taxpayer’s fixed-base percentage to account for a short taxable year.
3.3 The 16 percent cap and rounding
Whatever the historical ratio produced by the base-period calculation, the FBP may not exceed 16 percent (IRC § 41(c)(3)(C)).
4. The 50 percent minimum base amount
In no event shall the base amount be less than 50 percent of the QREs for the credit year (IRC § 41(c)(2)); the IRS Audit Techniques Guide restates this statutory floor.
5. Gross receipts: the denominator and the multiplier

For purposes of IRC § 41, gross receipts for any taxable year are reduced by returns and allowances made during the taxable year (IRC § 41(c)(6)). In the case of a foreign corporation, only gross receipts which are effectively connected with the conduct of a trade or business within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States are taken into account (IRC § 41(c)(6)). Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(c)(1) defines gross receipts broadly as the total amount, as determined under the taxpayer’s method of accounting, derived by the taxpayer from all its activities and from all sources (such as sales of inventory and services). Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(c)(2) lists specific items excluded from gross receipts, including returns or allowances; receipts from the sale or exchange of capital assets as defined in IRC § 1221; repayments of loans or similar instruments; receipts from a sale or exchange not in the ordinary course of business (such as the sale of an entire trade or business or of IRC § 1221(a)(2) depreciable property used in a trade or business); and certain sales and similar state and local taxes that are imposed directly on the purchaser and merely collected and remitted by the taxpayer. The IRS Audit Techniques Guide adds that gross receipts are not reduced by cost of goods sold and that examiners should confirm the same definition is applied consistently across every year. Additionally, if any of the four preceding taxable years used to calculate average annual gross receipts is a short taxable year, the gross receipts for that short year are annualized by multiplying the gross receipts for the short period by 12 and dividing the result by the number of months in the short taxable year (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(b)(2)).

Because gross receipts feed both the FBP denominator (in the historical base period) and the four-year average multiplier (in the current period), errors in either direction alter the base amount. Specifically, excluding non-operating items from base-period gross receipts reduces the denominator and increases the FBP, whereas excluding them from the preceding four years’ gross receipts reduces the multiplier and lowers the current base amount.
6. The consistency rule

Under the statutory consistency rule, the QREs taken into account in computing the FBP must be determined on a basis which is consistent with the determination of QREs for the credit year, without regard to whether the period for filing a claim for credit or refund has expired for any taxable year taken into account in determining the FBP (IRC § 41(c)(5)(A)). Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d)(1) applies this consistency mandate to both QREs and gross receipts in the base period, requires consistency without regard to the law in effect for the taxable years taken into account in computing the FBP, and applies it even if the statute of limitations for claiming a refund or assessing tax for those base-period years has expired. The IRS Audit Techniques Guide directs examiners to request and review base-period records to test consistency between current-year claims and base-period computations.
7. Controlled groups, acquisitions and dispositions

In determining the amount of the research credit under IRC § 41, all members of the same controlled group of corporations, and all trades or businesses (whether or not incorporated) which are under common control, are treated as a single taxpayer (IRC § 41(f)(1)(A)(i), (B)(i)). Consequently, the group’s base amount—including its FBP and four-year average gross receipts—is computed on an aggregate basis by combining the QREs and gross receipts of all group members after eliminating intra-group transactions (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6(b)), and the resulting group credit is allocated among the members in proportion to their respective current-year QREs (IRC § 41(f)(1)(A)(ii), (B)(ii)). When a major portion of a trade or business (or a separate unit thereof) is acquired or disposed of after the beginning of the measurement period, the statute requires symmetrical adjustments: the QREs and gross receipts of the acquiring taxpayer for all prior periods taken into account under IRC § 41 are increased by the amount of QREs and gross receipts attributable to the acquired portion of the business, and the QREs and gross receipts of the disposing predecessor are correspondingly decreased, provided the disposing taxpayer furnishes the necessary historical information to the acquirer (IRC § 41(f)(3)(A), (B)). The IRS Audit Techniques Guide notes that the IRC § 41(f)(5) control test uses a "more than 50 percent" ownership threshold rather than the "at least 80 percent" threshold used for consolidated return purposes under IRC § 1563(a), making the § 41 controlled group broader than a consolidated tax return group.
8. The base amount under the Alternative Simplified Credit

The Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) uses a fundamentally different base calculation. At the election of the taxpayer, the credit determined under IRC § 41(a)(1) equals 14 percent of so much of the QREs for the taxable year as exceeds 50 percent of the average QREs for the three taxable years preceding the taxable year for which the credit is being determined (IRC § 41(c)(4)(A)). Thus, the effective "base amount" under the ASC is simply 50 percent of the rolling three-year average of prior QREs. If the taxpayer has no QREs in any one of those three preceding taxable years, the credit rate is reduced to 6 percent of current-year QREs with no base subtraction (IRC § 41(c)(4)(B); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(c)(1)). Just as under the regular credit, the QREs taken into account for the three preceding taxable years must be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs for the credit year (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(c)(2)). Furthermore, if the credit year or any of the three preceding taxable years is a short taxable year, the QREs for the short taxable year are modified by annualizing or prorating based on the number of days in the short taxable year divided by 365 (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(c)(3)). Because the ASC base relies exclusively on the prior three years of QREs, it requires no 1984–1988 historical data and no gross receipts calculations.

cells: FBP (historical QREs ÷ gross receipts) × 4-year average gross receipts
14% (6% of QREs if no QREs in any of the 3 prior years)

body.text: 8.1 Electing and revoking the ASC

Current statutory and regulatory rules are more detailed. An election to use the ASC applies to the taxable year for which it is made and all succeeding taxable years unless revoked with the consent of the Secretary (IRC § 41(c)(4)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(b)(1)). Under final regulations issued in T.D. 9712 (applicable to elections for taxable years ending on or after February 27, 2015), a taxpayer may make an ASC election not only on a timely filed original return (including extensions) by completing the ASC section of Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities), but also on an amended return, provided the taxpayer has not previously claimed the IRC § 41 credit on an original or amended return for that taxable year and the period of limitations for assessment under IRC § 6501(a) has not expired for that year (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(b)(2)). However, a taxpayer that is a member of a controlled group may not make an ASC election on an amended return if any member of the controlled group previously claimed the research credit for that tax year using a method other than the ASC (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(b)(2)). Once made, an ASC election may be revoked for a subsequent taxable year only with the Commissioner’s consent, which is automatically deemed granted if the taxpayer completes the Regular Research Credit portion of Form 6765 on a timely filed original return (including extensions) for that year; an ASC election may not be revoked on an amended return (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(b)(3)).
8.2 When each base produces the larger credit (analysis)

That is an accurate mathematical reading of the statutory formulas: when a taxpayer’s RRC base amount is constrained by the 50 percent floor under IRC § 41(c)(2), the RRC yields exactly 10 percent of current-year QREs (20% × 50% of QREs), whereas a taxpayer with steady or growing QREs under the ASC may achieve an effective credit exceeding 7 percent of current-year QREs without having to prove 1980s gross receipts and QREs, and a taxpayer whose QREs have surged relative to its prior three-year average can earn up to nearly 14 percent of current QREs. Nevertheless, this comparison is mathematical analysis rather than a rule of law; the optimal election depends on each taxpayer’s exact financial figures and must be modeled on Form 6765.
9. Worked examples (all hypothetical)
Example A — RRC, base above the floor

Base-period QREs $2,000,000; base-period gross receipts $50,000,000. FBP = 2,000,000 ÷ 50,000,000 = 4.00%. Average gross receipts for prior 4 years = $100,000,000. Tentative base = 4.00% × $100,000,000 = $4,000,000. Current QREs = $6,000,000; 50% floor = $3,000,000. Base amount = $4,000,000 (greater of the two). Excess = $6,000,000 − $4,000,000 = $2,000,000. RRC = 20% × $2,000,000 = $400,000.
Example B — RRC, floor applies

FBP 3.00% (start-up, years 1–5). Average prior-4-year gross receipts $40,000,000. Tentative base = $1,200,000. Current QREs $5,000,000; floor = $2,500,000. Base amount = $2,500,000. Excess = $2,500,000. RRC = 20% × $2,500,000 = $500,000.
Example C — start-up year 6
Combined QREs for years 4 and 5 = $1,200,000; combined gross receipts for years 4 and 5 = $10,000,000. Ratio = 12.00%. FBP = 1/6 × 12.00% = 2.00%.
Example D — 16% cap
Base-period QREs $10,000,000 and gross receipts $50,000,000 give a ratio of 20.00%. The FBP used is capped at 16.00%.
Example E — ASC base

Prior three years’ QREs: $4,000,000, $5,000,000, $6,000,000; average = $5,000,000. ASC base = 50% × $5,000,000 = $2,500,000. Current QREs $6,000,000; excess = $3,500,000. ASC = 14% × $3,500,000 = $490,000. (Compare Example A, where the same $6,000,000 of current QREs produced a $400,000 RRC for a taxpayer with a 4.00% FBP and $100,000,000 of average gross receipts.)
11. A state credit that uses the federal base amount: Arizona

Arizona’s corporate and individual research and development tax credit (A.R.S. § 43-1168 and A.R.S. § 43-1074.01, administered by the Arizona Department of Revenue with refundable small-business portions certified by the Arizona Commerce Authority) is computed on the excess of qualified research expenses over the base amount "as defined in section 41(c)" of the Internal Revenue Code, with qualified research limited strictly to research conducted in Arizona (A.R.S. § 43-1168(A)). Arizona also allows taxpayers to elect the Alternative Simplified Credit method based on Arizona-sourced QREs. Under A.R.S. § 43-1168(A)(1), the tiered statutory rate schedule changes for later years:

headers: Taxable years beginning from and after December 31, 2030

cells: $600,000 plus 15% of the amount over $2.5 million
$500,000 plus 11% of the amount over $2.5 million

body.text: Hypothetical: Arizona excess QREs of $3,000,000. Before the change: $600,000 + 15% × $500,000 = $675,000. After: $500,000 + 11% × $500,000 = $555,000. Because the credit is a direct function of the excess of Arizona QREs over the Arizona-adapted IRC § 41(c) base amount, an accurate base amount calculation matters at the state level as well (analysis).
12. Key takeaways (analysis)

items: The RRC base amount = FBP × 4-year average gross receipts, but never less than 50% of current QREs; the FBP is capped at 16% and rounded to the nearest 1/100th of 1%.
The FBP comes from 1984–1988 data or, for start-ups, from a statutory 3%-then-phase-in schedule across years 1 through 11+.

Gross receipts and QREs must be defined the same way in the base period and the credit year under the IRC § 41(c)(5) consistency rule, and aggregated across controlled groups under IRC § 41(f)(1) with acquisition and disposition adjustments under IRC § 41(f)(3).

The ASC replaces the historical FBP and gross receipts formula with a base of 50% of the prior three years’ average QREs and a 14% credit rate (or 6% of current-year QREs with no base amount if the taxpayer had zero QREs in any of the three preceding taxable years).
